source.title: Sparsing Law: Towards Large Language Models with Greater Activation Sparsity
source.authors: Yuqi Luo; Chenyang Song; Xu Han; Yingfa Chen; Chao-Jun Xiao; Xiao-Jun Meng; Li-Qiong Deng; Jian-Sheng Wei; Zhi-Yuan Liu; Mao-Song Sun

record.tranche_reason: The study varies width-depth ratio and model scale and reports outcomes on training loss and downstream task scores. These bear on V4 and V6, but it does not test the original held-out-loss scaling laws or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper's main scaling results concern activation sparsity, not language-model loss. Its loss plots are training loss, not held-out loss; it does not fit loss power laws or test whether small-run loss fits predict larger runs. Its downstream scores are reported by model size, and its width-depth sweep reports limit training loss. Cited scaling-law results are not treated as this study's findings.
record.test_reason: The paper is about activation sparsity, but two side results bear on claim versions. A width-depth sweep at 0.1B reports limit training loss (V4). Dense downstream scores are reported across 0.1B–1.2B models (V6). Neither is fitted as a scaling law. The setting (µP Transformer, WSD schedule, decay stage with instruction data) is new relative to the originals.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that activation ratio follows convergent power-law (SiLU) or logspace power-law (ReLU) trends in training data. ReLU gives higher sparsity at comparable performance, and smaller stable width-depth ratios give sparser models. Limit sparsity is insensitive to scale, as confirmed at 2.4B. They draw no conclusions about loss scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures activation sparsity and its relation to data, architecture, and model scale, rather than fitting held-out loss scaling laws or optimizing parameters and tokens for a compute budget.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported width-depth effect changes at a bottleneck: activation ratio rises with width-depth ratio below about 114 for the 0.1B model and fluctuates around 8% above it; extremely small ratios harm training stability. The paper also notes that sparsity metrics relying on validation data can be sensitive to data distributions, but that concerns its activation-sparsity metric.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger models reach lower training loss and lower limit training loss (Figures 13–14); no power law is fitted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training loss decreases with parameter count across 0.1B–1.2B in a µP/WSD setup (no functional form given).

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The width-depth loss result is presented as a figure without numerical values in the text. Downstream scores are reported across a limited set of model sizes and are not fit to a predictive law; uncertainty estimates are not reported.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for Figures 13 and 14: their training-loss curves and limit-loss comparisons are figure-only and do not report held-out loss. No activation-sparsity results or cited results were included because they do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss in N, D or C. The figures show only training-loss curves and unfitted limit losses.
No extrapolation of loss from small runs; the 2.4B run is used only for sparsity extrapolation.
No compute-optimal allocation analysis; Chinchilla is cited only to justify a tokens/parameter axis.
Only depth/width at 0.1B, with ReLU and training loss. Other shape parameters (heads, FFN ratio, which is fixed at 2.5) and other scales are untested.
Other modalities, repeated data and fine-tuning are not tested.
No fitted predictive relationship between scale and scores, and no relation of scores to pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents for loss laws.

missing.what: Dense scores on complex benchmarks by size, mostly near random. ReLU average 13.6→18.3 and SiLU 13.7→18.9 across 0.1B–1.2B; MMLU stays at about 26 until 1.2B (33.4).
Per-benchmark dense scores by size, showing non-monotonic steps (BoolQ, COPA, WinoGrande).

record.verdict_notes: The loss and downstream results are incidental to a sparsity study. Downstream scores come from checkpoints after a decay stage that includes instruction data, not from pure pretraining. The per-row 'observed' states on cr/rc rows are single values; the V6 evidence lies in the trend across sizes, not in any one row. The width-depth range in the main runs is narrow (48–56).

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law fits and bottleneck conditions.
Whether fits from smaller runs predict loss of much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Only a 0.1B ReLU model's width-depth-ratio sweep is reported; other architectural choices and broader model scales are not tested at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer as tests of loss power laws.
The study reports downstream scores by model size, but does not fit a predictive relationship or relate scores to pretraining loss.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices and setup.

rows.subject: 0.1B ReLU-activated model
rows.operation_detail: Varied width-depth ratio across 9 settings and measured limit training loss.
rows.note: The text says an extremely small width-depth ratio causes significant performance degradation from training instability; it recommends a ratio in the stable interval, e.g. 74 to 282 for 0.1B. Figure values are not given in text.
rows.check: Measure is limit training loss (fitted to infinite data), not held-out loss. Values are figure-only; Figure 6's y-axis spans only about 3.40–3.50, so the loss spread across the 9 ratios is at most about 0.1. The text says only extremely small ratios degrade notably. Shape mostly matters little, with a failure at the extreme. Label as partial rather than a clear qualification.

rows.subject: Models from 0.1B to 1.2B
rows.operation_detail: Reported pre-training loss dynamics as training data and model size vary.
rows.value: The text states that larger models have smaller training loss; figure-only curve values.
rows.note: This is training loss, not the held-out loss specified by V1.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked. It reports training loss decreasing with size, with no power-law fit and no held-out loss. Figure 14's limit-loss-versus-parameters curve is also unfitted.

relationships.condition: Dense models 0.1B–1.2B, task-group averages (commonsense reasoning and reading comprehension), ReLU and SiLU
relationships.reason: C.R. averages rise monotonically (49.6→60.0 ReLU, 49.5→59.6 SiLU), as do R.C. averages (28.2→53.2, 27.7→54.8); cr_01–cr_10, rc_01–rc_10. Improvement is monotonic but no predictive law is fitted.
relationships.display_finding: Commonsense reasoning averages rise monotonically from 49.6 to 60.0 with ReLU and 49.5 to 59.6 with SiLU, while reading comprehension averages rise from 28.2 to 53.2 and 27.7 to 54.8, respectively.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Dense models 0.1B–1.2B, task-group averages (commonsense reasoning and reading comprehension), ReLU and SiLU
source_check.reason: Table 1 confirms monotonically increasing dense averages for both activations and task groups, including all stated endpoints. This supports improvement within the measured sweep; quantitative predictive accuracy is untested. Benchmark evaluation follows a decay stage incorporating instruction-tuning data.

relationships.reason: Based on text, since no rows capture these results. Some individual benchmarks are non-monotonic in size (e.g. BoolQ ReLU 60.8→56.3 at 0.2B; COPA ReLU 70→68 at 0.8B). Complex tasks stay near random; authors call them unreliable.
relationships.display_finding: ReLU BoolQ accuracy fell from 60.8 to 56.3 at 0.2B and COPA from 70 to 68 at 0.8B, while complex tasks remained near random.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Tables 4–5 confirm non-monotonic individual results: dense ReLU BoolQ falls from 60.8 to 56.3 between 0.1B and 0.2B, and COPA falls from 70.0 to 68.0 between 0.4B and 0.8B. Appendix K describes complex-task results as unreliable above random level. These qualify generalization beyond task-group averages.
